note: Does the pixel layer's own thermal conductivity confound the laser-cooling result, and should it be matched to the grease it replaces? Two identical runs differ only in mr_material: GAAS at 55 W/(m K), the device as built, and THERMAL_GREASE at 4, a counterfactual array with the incumbent TIM's conductivity. Same stack, same 200 um burial, same tiles, same plans, same hottest block (L3_4). Linear solves, no leakage feedback, uniform synthetic 100 W power map on the 7-core die -- so these are geometry and conductivity only.

passive_term.note: What the array is worth BEFORE any light. The k=4 arm is also the convection control: a 30 um grease layer under the same sink is exactly the incumbent stack.

finding.active_term: A LOW-conductivity pixel layer extracts MORE peak reduction per watt removed -- 1.21x for uniform, 1.24x for proportional, 1.38-1.61x for the targeted strategies. A high-k layer is nearly isothermal and well coupled to the sink, so a negative source in it is partly satisfied by drawing heat from the sink rather than from the die. Low k localises the extraction over the silicon.
finding.total: The device still wins decisively. At 30 W proportional the GaAs array reaches 68.01 C against the k-matched array's 86.37 C -- 18.36 K better -- because the 21.38 K passive term dwarfs the 24% it gives up on the active term. Measured against the convection control, total benefit is 33.72 K for GaAs versus 15.36 K k-matched, a factor of 2.2.
finding.implication: Pixel-layer conductivity is therefore a DESIGN VARIABLE with a genuine optimum, not a nuisance parameter to be normalised away: it trades the passive path against active coupling in opposite directions. Matching it to the grease would make the laser-cooling term look 24% better while making the part 18 K worse. Attribution is better handled with three arms -- convection control, array unpowered, array powered -- which isolates the laser term against the unpowered array without ever modelling a device nobody is building.
